Fit an edge weight model

Source: R/bison_model.R
bison_model.Rd

Fits a BISoN edge weight model, which estimates a posterior distribution for the edge weight of each dyad from observations of social events and the observation effort for each dyad. An edge weight is a dyad's underlying tendency to interact or associate, as a probability or a rate. The posterior distribution describes the values consistent with the data and priors, so edges observed rarely get wide uncertainty. This is usually the first step of an analysis: the fitted model is then used to plot the network, calculate network metrics and fit regressions.

Usage

bison_model(
  formula,
  data,
  model_type = c("binary", "count", "binary_conjugate", "count_conjugate"),
  directed = FALSE,
  partial_pooling = FALSE,
  zero_inflated = FALSE,
  priors = NULL,
  refresh = 0,
  mc_cores = 4,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  priors_only = FALSE,
  chains = 4,
  ...
)

Arguments

formula

A formula of the form (event | effort) ~ dyad(node_1, node_2). The left-hand side gives the column of social events (0/1 or counts) and the observation effort (a column, or a single number). Effort is how much each row was observed, such as the number of sampling periods or the hours of observation. The right-hand side gives the terms that explain the events. See Formula syntax below.

data

A data frame with one row per observation (disaggregated) or one row per dyad (aggregated).

model_type

The type of edge model: "binary" (events are present/absent in each sampling period, edge weights are probabilities), "count" (events are counts, edge weights are rates per unit effort), or the fast conjugate versions "binary_conjugate" and "count_conjugate", which only support a dyad() term.

directed

TRUE or FALSE: whether the network is directed. For undirected networks, rows for A-B and B-A refer to the same dyad.

partial_pooling

Whether to estimate the spread of edge weights from the data, so that information is shared between edges. How far estimates for dyads with few observations are pulled towards the mean of the edge prior then depends on how much edge weights vary across the network.

zero_inflated

Whether to use a zero-inflated model, for data with more zeros than the edge weights alone would predict (see the "stats" check in plot_predictions()). Zero inflation applies to each row of the data: each row has probability zero_prob of being a structural zero (a zero regardless of the edge weight). For binary data with one sampling period per row this can't be separated from the edge weights, so aggregate the data first.

priors

A list of priors, in the format returned by get_default_priors(). A prior describes which values of a parameter are plausible before seeing the data. If NULL, the defaults are used with a message; check them with prior_check() and prior_predictive_check().

refresh

How often the sampler prints progress (0 for silent).

mc_cores

Number of chains to run in parallel.

iter_sampling

Number of posterior draws to keep per chain, after warmup. For conjugate models, iter_sampling * chains draws are taken.

iter_warmup

Number of warmup iterations per chain, during which the sampler tunes itself. These draws are discarded.

priors_only

If TRUE, ignore the data and sample from the priors (used for prior predictive checks).

chains

Number of MCMC chains.

...

Further arguments passed to the $sample() method of cmdstanr::CmdStanModel, such as seed or adapt_delta.

Value

A bison_model object. Use summary.bison_model() or get_edgelist() to see the edge weights, plot_network() to visualise them, plot_trace() and plot_predictions() for diagnostics, and extract_metric() or bison_brm() for downstream analyses.

Details

Models other than the conjugate ones are fitted by MCMC (Markov chain Monte Carlo) in Stan, which draws samples from the posterior in several independent runs called chains. Conjugate models have a posterior that can be calculated exactly, so they are fitted in seconds without Stan, but they can't include other effects.

Formula syntax

  • dyad(node_1, node_2): estimate an edge weight for each dyad. The two columns hold node names or IDs. If they are both factors with the same levels, nodes that never appear in the data are kept.

  • x: a fixed effect of column x. Factors get one parameter per level.

  • (1 | g): a random intercept for each level of column g. Random effects are centred on 0, so a model without a dyad() term or factor fixed effect needs an intercept (1) to set the overall rate of events.

  • 1 or 0: include or exclude a global intercept (excluded by default).

Including other terms changes the interpretation of the edge weights, which then represent each dyad's tendency to interact after controlling for those effects. On the natural scale (e.g. in get_edgelist() and extract_metric()), they are the probability or rate for an observation in which the other effects (and any intercept) are 0, so continuous predictors may be easier to interpret if they are centred.

See also

get_default_priors(), prior_check(), summary.bison_model(), get_effects(), model_comparison(), bison_save()

Examples

sim_data <- simulate_bison_model("binary", aggregated = TRUE)
df <- sim_data$df_sim

# Fast conjugate model, no MCMC needed
fit_edge <- bison_model(
  (event | effort) ~ dyad(node_1_id, node_2_id),
  data = df,
  model_type = "binary_conjugate",
  priors = get_default_priors("binary_conjugate")
)
summary(fit_edge)

  (event | effort) ~ dyad(node_1_id, node_2_id),
  data = df,

  priors = get_default_priors("binary")
)
